title: LLD in Java: LRU cache, rate limiter, parking lot
seriesTitle: Interview roadmap: Java and Spring Boot
seriesDescription: Java and Spring Boot interview topics in JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short Java/SQL code and multi-correct questions. Java only: nothing here mixes in Python.
description: Low-level design in Java: an LRU cache on LinkedHashMap, a thread-safe token bucket class, a parking lot with interfaces, design patterns and thread-safety follow-ups.
source: Oracle Java docs (LinkedHashMap, interfaces); Effective Java (Item 3); Head First Design Patterns; Grokking the OOD interview problem lists; LeetCode 146 discussion

questions.prompt: Write a generic Java class LRU<K,V> extending LinkedHashMap that keeps at most cap entries, evicting the least recently used one (cap is a constructor argument).
questions.explanation: accessOrder = true makes get() move an entry to the end. The interview follow-up is to implement the same with a HashMap plus a doubly linked list with head and tail sentinels, giving O(1) get and put.

questions.prompt: Write a thread-safe Java class TokenBucket(double capacity, double refillPerSecond) with a boolean tryAcquire() method that refills lazily from elapsed time (never above capacity), starts full and takes one token on success.

checks.label: caps tokens at capacity with Math.min

questions.explanation: Lazy refill avoids a timer thread. Use nanoTime (monotonic) rather than wall-clock time. Other correct versions use a lock or an AtomicLong with compare-and-set.

questions.prompt: Write Java for a parking lot: an interface Vehicle with an int method spotsNeeded(), and a concrete class Car that implements Vehicle and needs 1 spot.
questions.explanation: Code to the interface so a Bike or Truck can be added without touching the lot. An abstract class is the alternative when the vehicles share state or behaviour, and an enum VehicleType is the usual way to tag them. Other correct versions exist, such as an abstract class with an abstract method.

questions.prompt: An LRU cache has capacity 3. Operations: put(1), put(2), put(3), get(1), put(4), get(3), put(5). What is the sum of the keys left in the cache?
questions.explanation: After put(4) key 2 is evicted; after get(3) the order is 1,4,3 (oldest first); put(5) evicts 1. Remaining keys 4, 3, 5 sum to 12.

questions.prompt: A token bucket has capacity 5 and refills 2 tokens per second. It starts full, 5 requests are accepted at t = 0, then 10 requests arrive at t = 1.5 s (all at the same instant). How many of those 10 are accepted?
questions.explanation: 1.5 s x 2 tokens/s = 3 tokens were refilled, so 3 requests succeed and 7 are rejected.

questions.prompt: Match each parking-lot or cache design need to the pattern that fits best.

left.text: Switch between hourly and flat pricing or LRU and LFU eviction
Create the right Spot subclass from a type
Update display boards when a spot is taken
A ticket moves from ISSUED to PAID to EXITED

questions.explanation: Name the pattern only after stating the problem it solves. Strategy is the most frequent LLD answer (pricing, eviction, rate-limiting algorithm).

questions.prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the option that describes them correctly.
questions.assertion: An LRU cache built from a hash map and a doubly linked list supports O(1) get and put.
questions.reason: The map finds a node directly and the doubly linked list can unlink and move it without scanning.

whys.a: Right: lookup is O(1) via the map and reordering is O(1) via the list pointers.

questions.explanation: A singly linked list would need the previous node to unlink, forcing an O(n) search.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the option that describes them correctly.
questions.assertion: Define PricingPolicy as an interface so the parking lot can swap pricing rules.
questions.reason: The compiler rejects new PricingPolicy() because an interface cannot be instantiated directly.

whys.a: The instantiation rule does not explain why an interface helps with swapping.
whys.b: Right: both true, but swapping comes from programming to an interface, not from the ban on instantiating it.

questions.explanation: Inject the policy through the constructor so tests can pass a fake.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the option that describes them correctly.
questions.assertion: LinkedHashMap with accessOrder = true is a convenient base for an LRU cache.
questions.reason: LinkedHashMap is thread-safe, so concurrent get calls are safe.

whys.c: Right: LinkedHashMap is not thread-safe and in access order even get() mutates it.
whys.d: The assertion is the true statement.

questions.explanation: Wrap with Collections.synchronizedMap or guard get and put with one lock. Caffeine is the production answer.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the option that describes them correctly.
questions.assertion: The Spot class should compute the parking fee for the vehicle it holds.
questions.reason: The Single Responsibility Principle says a class should have one reason to change.

whys.d: Right: pricing changes for business reasons unrelated to spots, so the assertion is false while the reason is true.

questions.explanation: Put pricing in a PricingPolicy used by the Ticket or a payment service.

questions.text: LinkedHashMap is constructed with access order {1}, you override {2}, and the eviction test is size() {3} cap.
questions.explanation: The three-argument constructor is LinkedHashMap(initialCapacity, loadFactor, accessOrder). removeEldestEntry is called after each put and returns true when the eldest entry should go.

questions.prompt: Why is a plain LinkedHashMap LRU unsafe for concurrent readers even if the threads only call get?

options.text: get() reorders entries, so each read mutates it
options.why: Right: concurrent reorders can corrupt the links or lose entries.
It is not guaranteed to throw; corruption can be silent.

options.text: LinkedHashMap forbids more than one reader thread at any time
options.why: No such restriction exists in the class.

options.text: The hash function differs per thread
options.why: Hashing is deterministic and does not depend on the thread.

questions.explanation: Use a lock around get and put, or a concurrent cache library such as Caffeine.

questions.prompt: Which are sound LLD practices for the parking lot? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use an enum for VehicleType rather than free strings
options.why: Right: it is type-safe and exhaustive.

options.text: Inject the pricing and allocation strategies through constructors
Return Optional<Spot> from findSpot instead of null
options.why: Right: the absence case is explicit.

options.text: Expose a public mutable List<Spot> field for convenience
options.why: Callers could corrupt the lot state; expose behaviour instead.

questions.explanation: Clarify requirements, list entities, define interfaces, then write the core flow park and unpark first.

questions.prompt: True or false: a double-checked locking Singleton in Java needs its instance field declared volatile so another thread cannot see a partially constructed object.

options.why: Right: without volatile the write of the reference can be reordered before the constructor's writes, so a second thread may see a half-built object (fixed by the Java 5 memory model with volatile).
Incorrect: the synchronized block only protects the second check; the unsynchronised first read can still observe a reference to an unfinished object without volatile.

questions.explanation: Cleaner alternatives are the initialisation-on-demand holder idiom or a single-element enum Singleton (Effective Java, Item 3), neither of which needs volatile.

questions.prompt: True or false: a non-abstract Java class that implements an interface but leaves one of its abstract methods unimplemented still compiles.

options.why: Incorrect: the compiler reports that the class must be declared abstract or implement the method.
Right: a concrete class must implement every abstract method of its interfaces, or be declared abstract itself.

questions.explanation: This compile-time check is what makes interfaces a safe seam for swapping strategies: nothing can be wired in half-finished.
